findings.title: verify-email page is missing meta robots=noindex and Referrer-Policy hardening — reset/verify tokens may leak to search-engine indices and outbound links
findings.description: Both reset-password.vue and verify-email.vue read a single-use token from `route.query.token` (reset-password.vue:9-12, verify-email.vue:11-14). Tech-spec acknowledges this is the standard pattern. However, because these two pages render the token-bearing URL directly from the address bar with NO `useHead`/`useSeoMeta` block, the framework default applies: pages are crawler-indexable and `Referrer-Policy` defaults to whatever the browser policy is (commonly `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, which still leaks the FULL URL — including the token query — to same-origin outbound links and is enough to leak path+query in many cross-origin redirect chains). Concrete leak vectors: (1) a user pastes the password-reset URL into a chat client that opens an unfurl/preview bot — the bot fetches the URL from its own egress, the page is rendered, and the token is consumed by the bot, not the human. The backend reset-token is one-use, so the legitimate user then sees an 'invalid link' page with no recovery path. (2) Search engines that ingest URLs from referer logs of third-party sites can index `/auth/reset-password?token=…` if the user ever clicks an outbound link from the reset page — neither auth page sets `noindex`. (3) Browser history sync (Chrome Sync, Firefox Sync) replicates the full URL across the user's other devices, broadening the exposure window before single-use consumption. Note `frontend/nuxt.config.ts` does not set a default `routeRules` policy or `app.head` referrer policy. While this is a known tradeoff with backend-issued URL tokens (and cannot be fully eliminated without a token-exchange flow), the cheap mitigations are not in place.
findings.impact: Increases the window/surface for single-use token leakage. Verify-email tokens are lower stakes (consume = email confirmed), but reset-password tokens grant full account takeover for their TTL. Bot/preview consumption is the most realistic vector — chat platforms (Slack, Telegram, iMessage) routinely fetch URLs server-side, and if a bot consumes the token first, the user is locked out of password reset until requesting a new link. Sync-replicated history broadens the window if the user's account on another device is later compromised.
findings.recommendation: Add to `nuxt.config.ts` under `app.head.meta`: `{ name: 'robots', content: 'noindex, nofollow' }` for auth routes (or use `routeRules: { '/auth/**': { robots: 'noindex, nofollow', headers: { 'Referrer-Policy': 'no-referrer' } } }`). Per-page hardening is also acceptable: in reset-password.vue and verify-email.vue add `useHead({ meta: [{ name: 'robots', content: 'noindex, nofollow' }, { name: 'referrer', content: 'no-referrer' }] })`. The `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` ensures any link click from the token-bearing page omits the URL from outbound requests entirely. A defense-in-depth follow-up (tracked separately): on reset-password.vue mount, replace the URL via `history.replaceState` to strip `?token=` from the address bar after capturing it into in-memory state — reduces sync/screenshot leakage. Tech-spec Decision 12 already commits to OWASP A05 hardening; this completes that posture for the URL-token surface.
findings.cwe: CWE-598 (Use of GET Request Method With Sensitive Query Strings), CWE-200 (Exposure of Sensitive Information)

findings.category: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
findings.title: forgot-password.vue swallows ALL errors silently (network, 5xx, CSRF) — operators cannot distinguish 'service down' from 'success' on the frontend
findings.description: `onSubmit` in forgot-password.vue:21-31 wraps the API call in a bare `try { … } catch {}` (line 27-29) with no logging, no Sentry hook, no error event emitted. The comment correctly states 'Always present a successful state to avoid revealing whether the email exists' — that is the right anti-enumeration UX. But the same `catch {}` also silently swallows: (a) network failures (backend down), (b) 500 errors, (c) CSRF-token validation failures (e.g. an attacker who scraped the form with no XSRF cookie), (d) CORS misconfigurations after a deploy. From the user's perspective, the screen always says 'Якщо акаунт … існує, ви отримаєте лист' — but if the request never reached the backend, no email is queued. Operators monitoring the UX have no signal here; only backend logs reveal there was no `forgot_password_requested` event for that minute. This is operational-monitoring debt, not a direct vulnerability — but it diverges from the rest of the codebase (login/register/reset/verify all branch on status code).
findings.impact: Operations and monitoring blind spot. A regression that breaks /api/auth/forgot-password (e.g. SMTP outage handled with 503, broken CSRF after Decision 12 rollout) will produce zero frontend-side telemetry. Users never see an error; ops sees a quiet drop in `forgot_password_requested` events and may not correlate it. Worth one minor-severity entry because the file's comment says 'success state' but it actually means 'success appearance even when nothing succeeded.'
findings.recommendation: Two non-leaking options: (1) keep UX identical (always show success) but emit a frontend telemetry event (`useNuxtApp().$logger?.warn('forgot-password request failed', ...)` or future Sentry hook) so monitoring catches infrastructure failures; (2) at minimum, branch on status code so 5xx/network errors show a generic 'try again later' message — 200, 4xx (except 429), and 429 all map to the same anti-enumeration success message; only 5xx/network failure differs. Anti-enumeration is preserved because the success message is shown for both 200 and 4xx — only operational failures (5xx/network) diverge, and an attacker cannot enumerate via 5xx. Document the choice in tech-spec Decision 7's neighbourhood.

findings.title: verify-email cooldown timer is hard-coded to 60s and ignores backend Retry-After / actual remaining-window — desync on 429
findings.description: verify-email.vue:88-107 calls `startCooldown(60)` on BOTH the success path (line 96) and the 429 path (line 102). Backend resend rate-limit (per Decision 7) uses Redis `SET NX EX 60`, so 60s is correct on a freshly-issued lock — but on a 429 from the user's *first* press in this tab, the user may already be N seconds into an existing 60s lock from another tab/device/page-navigation, in which case the displayed countdown is too long. Also, if backend ever tunes the window (Decision 7 doesn't pin the value as forever-60s), the frontend silently drifts. Backend should be the source of truth via `Retry-After` header (RFC 9110 §10.2.3) on the 429 response, and the frontend should parse it.
findings.location: frontend/pages/auth/verify-email.vue:96, 102 (both call `startCooldown(60)` with a magic number)
findings.impact: UX degradation, not a security gap (backend rate-limit is the real guard, as the audit task brief acknowledges). User may wait longer than necessary, or — in the opposite case if backend ever shortens the window — try too early and get another 429. The audit notes 'rate-limiting bypass' as a focus area; the cooldown is correctly client-only (per Decision 7) and the backend enforces, so there is no bypass per se — this is just the desync.
findings.recommendation: Read `Retry-After` from the 429 response if present: `const retryAfter = err?.response?.headers?.get?.('Retry-After'); startCooldown(parseInt(retryAfter, 10) || 60)`. On the success path, 60 is fine because the lock is freshly issued. Backend implementation note: ensure the resend-verification 429 path emits `Retry-After: <seconds-remaining>` derived from `TTL` of the Redis key. (This is a backend tweak; flagged here because the frontend-side fix is the consumption.)
findings.cwe: CWE-1287 (Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input) — broadly: hard-coded coupling to a backend constant

findings.title: register.vue 409 message reveals account existence — anti-enumeration breach for the registration endpoint
findings.description: register.vue:51-52: `if (code === 409) submitError.value = 'Користувач з таким email вже існує. …'`. This is the standard registration UX, and tech-spec/user-spec do not currently mandate anti-enumeration on registration — but it's worth surfacing because the auth task brief explicitly lists 'Anti-enumeration' as a focus area, and the inconsistency is real: forgot-password is enumeration-safe (always-200), but register telegraphs `409 → email exists`. An attacker who collects a list of corporate emails can determine which already have accounts, then pivot to the forgot-password endpoint on those addresses (or to the login brute-force, which has Decision 4 dual-key protection but still allows steady probing). This is a documented industry tradeoff (Auth0, GitHub, Google all return distinct 'account exists' on signup); flagging as `minor` since it's a deliberate UX choice, not an oversight, but the asymmetry with forgot-password should be conscious.
findings.location: frontend/pages/auth/register.vue:51-52; backend behavior — POST /api/auth/register returning 409 on duplicate email
findings.impact: Email enumeration via registration form. Mitigated in production by the existence of forgot-password as an alternate enumeration vector — meaning fixing register-side enumeration alone does not close the attack. If the project later wants full anti-enumeration parity (e.g. for a high-value B2B target list), the registration flow would need to switch to 'we sent you a confirmation email' + email-side branching (account exists → 'login' link; account new → verify) — a meaningful redesign.
findings.recommendation: Decision needed at the spec level, not the code level. Option A (status quo): document in tech-spec that registration deliberately reveals account existence for UX, and accept the asymmetry. Option B: switch to email-channel disambiguation (always 200 on /register; email 'account exists, click here to log in' vs 'finish setup'). Option B is heavier but consistent with forgot-password's posture. Either way, make the call deliberately and pin it in a Decision so it isn't drift.

findings.title: Login page does not pre-populate email after successful registration redirect — minor UX, but check that ?registered=1 / ?reset=1 / ?verified is never reflected unsafely
findings.description:
register.vue:47 navigates to `/auth/login?registered=1` and reset-password.vue:50 navigates to `/auth/login?reset=1`. login.vue does not currently read these query params (no `useRoute()` import, no banner rendered) — so they're inert. This is a defense-in-depth note: when a future task adds 'You've registered successfully — please log in' or 'Password updated — please log in' banners on login.vue, the implementer must NOT do `

{{ route.query.message }}

` reflectively. Vue's `{{ }}` would auto-escape HTML entities (good against stored XSS), but a value like `'http://evil.example.com'` rendered as link text or used in a `:href` would still allow open-redirect / phishing-banner attacks. The current code is fine; flagging now to prevent regression.
findings.location: frontend/pages/auth/login.vue:1-115 (does not read query); frontend/pages/auth/register.vue:47; frontend/pages/auth/reset-password.vue:50
findings.impact: No exploit today. Forward-looking guardrail to prevent the pattern from being extended unsafely. The two query keys in use (`registered=1`, `reset=1`) are static literals set by our own code, so no untrusted input reaches the URL today.
findings.recommendation: When adding banners triggered by these flags, treat the query value as a boolean flag only — do NOT render `route.query.message` content. Render fixed Ukrainian strings keyed by a fixed enum: `if (route.query.registered === '1') showRegisteredBanner = true`. Add a code-review note to the auth README or to tech-spec Decision 9 vicinity. Optionally strip the query after read with `router.replace({ query: {} })` so refreshing the page doesn't re-show the banner.
findings.cwe: CWE-79 (Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation) — preventive note

findings.title: auth pages render without a top-level error boundary — uncaught render error in 3rd-party (vee-validate / zod) leaks stack to user
findings.description: All five pages use `useForm` and `toTypedSchema(schema)` directly at module top level (e.g. login.vue:14-17). If `@vee-validate/zod` ever throws synchronously during component setup (version skew, peer-dep break), Nuxt's default error page renders the error stack to the user. Stack traces from auth pages can include path strings, env hints, or library internals that aid an attacker in reconnaissance. There's no `<NuxtErrorBoundary>` wrapping these pages and no top-level `app.vue` error handler. This is generic Nuxt hardening, not a Task-10-specific bug, but the auth surface is the highest-value page set for stack-leak reconnaissance.
findings.location: frontend/app.vue:1-6 (no error boundary); frontend/layouts/auth.vue:1-8 (no error handling); all five pages in frontend/pages/auth/
findings.impact: Reconnaissance aid in error scenarios. Not directly exploitable. Most relevant during dev/staging where stack-trace-rich error pages are common; production builds do strip some detail by default but not all framework errors.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the slot in `layouts/auth.vue` with `<NuxtErrorBoundary>` rendering a generic 'Сталась помилка' fallback and emitting the error to telemetry. Production-side: ensure `nuxt.config.ts` sets `nitro.errorHandler` or relies on Nuxt's default production error page (which is generic). Verify that `NODE_ENV=production` is set in CI deploy so framework error pages don't leak. Low priority but cheap to add.
findings.cwe: CWE-209 (Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information)
